To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) APR is a major abdominal procedure that is associated with significant morbidity and mortality; 2) the procedure can be performed with acceptable mortality and morbidity rates; 3) APR is associated with high rates of sexual and urinary dysfunction; and 4) APR is associated, on average, with a worse overall survival than sphincter-preserving procedures.
APR for rectal cancer can be performed with excellent results, with a low rate of local recurrence and acceptable survival, when performed with the principles of TME and ANP.
The overall survival rate was 60% and the local recurrence rate 12.8% for 148 patients who underwent APR for rectal cancer in accordance with the principle of TME and ANP.

APR for low rectal cancer performed according to the principles of TME and ANP is a safe procedure with low morbidity and mortality and good long term results.
